newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Farm ministers to discuss 97/98 prices on TuesDAY.
newsitem.headline: Farm ministers to discuss 97/98 prices on TuesDAY.

text.p: European Union farm ministers will hold a preliminary discussion on Tuesday on a proposal to keep most farm prices unchanged in 1997/98 but slash aid payments to cereals and oilseed farmers by 1.4 billion ecus.
"Ministers are likely to raise lots of objections, notably on the arable aid cuts," a Dutch EU presidency official said, adding there was no urgency to reach a decision.

EU sources said that the televised ministerial debate on Tuesday afternoon would probably follow a traditional pattern with ministers attacking any cutbacks and presenting shopping lists of "sweeteners" for farmers.
Agreement is not usually reached until June.

The European Commission proposed some minor changes on March 5 that would save 82 million Ecus from the 1998 budget of just over 41 billion Ecus. The changes included: - Reduction in monthly intervention cereals storage payments by nine percent to 1.0 ecu a tonne to take account of lower interest rates. - Reduction in the monthly sugar storage refund by 17 percent to 0.35 ecu per 100 kg also in view of lower interest rates. - Reduction in the monthly intervention rice storage increments by 12 percent to 2.0 ecus a tonne.

The intervention price for paddy rice would be cut by five percent to 333.45 ecus a tonne. - Flax and hemp area aid payments would be cut by 5.7 percent to 815.86 ecus per hectare and by 7.5 percent to 716.63 ecus per hectare. A flax promotional levy of 49.62 ecus per ha would be reduced to zero.

The 1.4 billion ecu cut in cereals, oilseeds and protein crop compensatory payments was originally proposed in the summer of 1996 to help pay for an emergency beef aid package following the mad cow crisis but was rejected by farm ministers.
Cereals and oilseed payments would be cut by 7.3 percent and 4.8 percent respectively and set-aside payments by 26.8 percent.
But France, Germany and many other member states are likely to strongly oppose such a move.
